title: Prologue
focus: the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus speaks a sonnet: two households of equal rank in Verona break out in new violence from an old grudge; from them come a pair of 'star-cross'd lovers' whose deaths end their parents' strife. The play, the Chorus says, will show 'the two hours' traffic of our stage.'

context.history: Elizabethan plays sometimes opened with a Chorus or Prologue. The sonnet was the fashionable love-poem form of the 1590s; Shakespeare's own sonnets were circulating among friends by 1598.

significance: Telling the ending first turns the play from a story of what happens into a study of how and why, and makes every hopeful moment dramatically ironic.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Prologue,” how does Shakespeare show the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the structure you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Prologue, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the structure in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Prologue develops the idea of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Prologue (where it begins, turns and ends) and its structure shape the reader's understanding of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Prologue suggests about the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's structure and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses structure in Prologue to complicate the reader's understanding of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Prologue within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Prologue alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold follows or bends those conventions, using the structure as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Prologue and its treatment of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's structure and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Prologue as evidence for a larger claim about the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Prologue as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the Prologue's sonnet and the ending foretold. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

satQuestions.passage:
Two households, both alike in dignity,
In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life;
Whose misadventured piteous overthrows
Do with their death bury their parents’ strife.
The fearful passage of their death-mark’d love,
And the continuance of their parents’ rage,
Which, but their children’s end, nought could remove,
Is now the two hours’ traffic of our stage;

What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.

literaryElements.label: Structure
literaryElements.explanation: The Prologue is a sonnet (fourteen lines, abab cdcd efef gg) spoken by the Chorus: the play opens with a love poem about death.

literaryElements.label: Foreshadowing
literaryElements.explanation: It tells the whole ending: the lovers "take their life" and their deaths "bury their parents' strife."

literaryElements.label: Diction / vocabulary
literaryElements.explanation: "civil blood makes civil hands unclean": the repeated word turns "civil" (of citizens; polite) against itself.

themesAndDevelopment.development: "star-cross'd" and "death-mark'd" suggest fate; ask whether the rest of the play agrees.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: haste and time
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Everything happens too fast: a four-day action, a marriage the day after meeting, a wedding moved up a day; Friar Laurence warns "they stumble that run fast." In this scene: “their children’s end, nought could remove, / Is now the two hours’ traffic of our stage; / The which if you with patient ears” (Prologue, speech (speech 0)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: death as bridegroom
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Death is repeatedly imagined as Juliet's husband or lover, long before she lies in the tomb. Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Prologue”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The Chorus speaks a sonnet: two households of equal rank in Verona break out in new violence from an old grudge; from them come a pair of 'star-cross'd lovers' whose deaths end their parents' strife. The play, the Chorus says, will show 'the two hours' traffic of our stage.'

Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

items.text: How does “Prologue” build on “Dramatis Personae”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous scene.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: By revealing the ending at the start, the Prologue shifts the audience's attention from what happens to why and how. Useful evidence: “A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life” (Prologue, speech (speech 0)): The lovers are thwarted by the stars; "take their life" means both "are born" and "kill themselves." On structure: The Prologue is a sonnet (fourteen lines, abab cdcd efef gg) spoken by the Chorus: the play opens with a love poem about death. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
